claims.quote: UTC− browsers display Python dates one day early

known_problems.reason: Says users west of UTC see Python-supplied dates one day early and min_date/max_date limits shifted (route 1 of GT-l1), and faults the cause: 'subtracting a positive local offset moves that timestamp into the preceding UTC day before the ISO date is extracted'.

claims.notes: Situation: a DatePicker whose value/min_date/max_date come from Python, shown in a browser west of UTC. Says the displayed day and the bounds are one day early. True: Python's Date property turns every date or string into a date and serializes it as UTC-midnight milliseconds; the head's _unlocal_date subtracts getTimezoneOffset()*60000 (positive west of UTC) before taking toISOString()'s UTC day, so the instant falls into the previous UTC day. This is GT-l1's midnight route, so the known problem settles questions 2 to 4.
evidence: clone/bokehjs/src/lib/models/widgets/date_picker.ts: render() passes value/min_date/max_date through _unlocal_date, which subtracts the timezone offset before toISOString().substr(0, 10).
clone/bokeh/core/property/datetime.py: Date.transform parses strings and numbers into datetime.date, which is serialized as a millisecond timestamp.
references.json GT-l1 mechanism records the run (date(2019, 9, 20) gives 2019-09-19 in America/New_York). My own node run was refused by the tool (no encoded focused-command allowance).

anchors.quote: Preserve the intended calendar date when building Pikaday's local Date: use UTC year/month/day for numeric UTC-midnight Date-property values, and local year/month/day for the date strings produced by _on_select, instead of shifting every timestamp by getTimezoneOffset().
Preserve the date's intended calendar components when converting it to Pikaday's local Date.

sufficiency.reason: The fix splits by type: numeric (Python-supplied) values take their UTC year/month/day, which is the commit-before behaviour that GT-l1 records as giving the Python-written day for every time of day in every zone, so routes 1-3 are cured; strings from _on_select (toDateString, parsed as local midnight) take local components, so the clicked day stays correct east of UTC and the #9129 bug does not return.
evidence: references.json GT-l1 mechanism: before the change all 48 half-hours give 2019-09-20 in all nine zones

safety.reason: No run could be made (the focused-command tool refused node). By reading, one case is uncertain: a string value set from JS (e.g. an ISO 'YYYY-MM-DD' string from CustomJS) would be parsed as UTC midnight and, with local components, show a day early west of UTC; whether such uses exist or matter was not checked.

claims.quote: UTC− initial dates shift back one day

known_problems.reason: Says Python-supplied initial selection and min/max bounds are 'reconstructed one calendar day early, so users can see or select the wrong date' in UTC− zones, and faults the cause: 'subtracting the positive local offset moves them into the previous UTC day'.

claims.notes: Situation: Python-supplied DatePicker values and bounds in a browser west of UTC. Says the initial selection and bounds land one day early. True: Python sends UTC-midnight milliseconds; the head's _unlocal_date subtracts the positive offset before taking the UTC day. This is GT-l1's midnight route, so the known problem settles questions 2 to 4.
evidence: clone/bokehjs/src/lib/models/widgets/date_picker.ts: _unlocal_date subtracts getTimezoneOffset()*60000 before toISOString().substr(0, 10); render() applies it to value, min_date and max_date.
clone/bokeh/core/property/datetime.py: Date.transform yields datetime.date values serialized as milliseconds.
references.json GT-l1 mechanism records the run; my own node run was refused by the tool.

anchors.quote: Preserve the UTC calendar date for epoch-millisecond inputs and apply local-date correction only to values known to have come from local date strings; preferably pass an unambiguous date-only representation through this conversion.

sufficiency.reason: Every epoch-millisecond input (all Python-supplied values, whatever their time of day) keeps its UTC calendar date, which GT-l1 records as the Python-written day in every zone, curing routes 1-3; the local correction stays for the _on_select strings, so the clicked day remains right east of UTC. The alternative of an unambiguous date-only representation is the route GT-l1's obligation names (#9509).

safety.reason: No run could be made (the focused-command tool refused node). How 'values known to have come from local date strings' are recognised is left open, and a JS-set ISO date string would be misread west of UTC if treated as local; the date-only alternative changes serialization, whose effect on Python callbacks was not checked.

claims.quote: UTC− zones display Python date values one day early

known_problems.reason: Says users west of UTC 'can see the selected value, and the picker limits, one day earlier than configured when the DatePicker receives a Python date', and faults the cause: 'in a UTC−5 browser this subtraction moves that instant to the prior UTC day'.

claims.notes: Situation: a Python date given to a DatePicker, viewed in a browser west of UTC (UTC−5 example). Says value and limits display one day early. True: Python serializes a date as UTC-midnight milliseconds and the head's _unlocal_date subtracts the positive offset before taking the UTC day. This is GT-l1's midnight route, so the known problem settles questions 2 to 4.
evidence: clone/bokehjs/src/lib/models/widgets/date_picker.ts: _unlocal_date subtracts the offset; render() applies it to value, min_date and max_date.
clone/bokeh/core/property/datetime.py: Date values serialized as milliseconds.
references.json GT-l1 mechanism records the run in America/New_York; my own node run was refused by the tool.

anchors.quote: Normalize the source date without subtracting the browser offset from UTC-midnight timestamp values
Preserve the calendar date of UTC-midnight model values while normalizing client-selected local date strings.

sufficiency.reason: Not subtracting the offset from UTC-midnight timestamps while keeping the correction for client-selected strings cures the midnight route (dates, midnight datetimes and strings west of UTC, plus bounds) without bringing back the east-of-UTC click bug. The fix names only UTC-midnight values, and says nothing of Python datetimes that carry a time of day, which GT-l1 routes 2 and 3 shift to the adjacent day; as worded it does not ensure those are cured.

safety.reason: No run could be made (the focused-command tool refused node). How client strings and model values are told apart is not specified; a JS-set ISO date string treated as a local string would be misread west of UTC, which was not checked.
